title: Anduril Is Building a Prime. The Price Assumes a Platform.
displayTitle: Anduril is building a prime. The price assumes a platform.
seoTitle: Anduril Valuation: The $61 Billion Capital Productivity Bet
seoDescription: A sourced October 2026 Anduril valuation models factories, software margins, cash needs and minority interests, with a reproducible DCF and reverse valuation.
subtitle: A cash-flow valuation of the factories, software economics, and financing required to turn defense demand into shareholder returns.
author: Sulayman Bowles
ledeMarkdown:
On July 27, the first Ohio-built Fury aircraft rolled off Anduril’s Arsenal-1 production line. A completed aircraft is evidence. A factory’s advertised annual capacity is still a promise. The distinction matters when the company behind both commands a $61 billion financing valuation. [S8](#source-s8) [S1](#source-s1)

My view is that Anduril can become a major defense supplier without being a good investment at that price. The opportunity is real: connect weapons through common software, build more of them, and shorten the interval between design and delivery. The investment question is harder: how much of that improvement belongs to shareholders after development spending, factories, inventory, and the government’s bargaining power?

I underwrite approximately **$28 billion of consolidated enterprise value** in the base case. Adding an assumed $3 billion of net cash produces about **$31 billion of gross equity value, before minority interests and other senior claims**. That is not a liquidation estimate or a price for a particular share class. It already assumes annual revenue reaches roughly $51 billion in 2036 and operating margins reach 22%. The gap to the financing price is not a forecast that Anduril fails. It is the cost of waiting for a very large business to generate distributable cash.
thesis: Anduril’s strongest advantage may be capital productivity, not software-style lock-in. At $61 billion, investors need the economics of the upside case, not merely a successful new defense prime.
evidenceBoundary: Evidence cutoff: October 14, 2026. Company announcements, media-reported projections, and author assumptions are distinguished. No audited Anduril accounts, current cash balance, share-class terms, or completed Arsenal-2 minority-interest agreement were available in the reviewed record. All values are USD; model figures are billions. The DCF values consolidated operations. Gross equity bridges are conditional and precede minority-interest and security-specific adjustments.
assumptions: FY2025 revenue is company-reported; FY2026 revenue is a March investor projection reported by the press, not an observed result or a newly confirmed October forecast.
The model uses a remaining-2026 stub, annual forecasts through 2036, a five-year maturity transition, and a reinvestment-funded terminal value.
Net cash and available liquidity are separate $3 billion assumptions. The zero minority-interest input means an unadjusted gross bridge, not proof that minority interests have no value.

sections.title: Start with the price that actually closed
paragraphs: The completed May financing raised $5 billion at a $61 billion valuation; Anduril reported $2.2 billion of 2025 revenue. Reuters subsequently reported discussions about financing near $100 billion, potentially with performance conditions. A conversation about a round is not a closed round. I use $61 billion as the transaction reference and $100 billion as an additional expectations test. [S1](#source-s1) [S2](#source-s2)

The operating record is less complete than the funding record. Press reporting in March put projected 2026 sales at $4.3 billion. The Information separately reported projected operating losses of $1.2 billion. Neither is an audited 2026 result. The sales anchor is seven months old; new awards do not automatically turn it into a higher recognized-revenue figure. [S4](#source-s4) [S3](#source-s3)

This is an expectations model rather than a disguised claim to inside information. I do not know product-level gross margins, the funded backlog, customer-advance balances, warranty provisions, or the current capital structure. Those omissions rule out a credible per-share appraisal. They do not prevent asking what operating outcome would make the headline price sensible.

table.caption: The public numbers are not interchangeable
rows: Enterprise value or common-share fair value
Actual October revenue or recurring software sales
Five-year base plus a five-year option
Funded backlog or $2bn of annual revenue

sections.title: The valuable part is the system, but the bill includes the hardware
paragraphs: The strongest Anduril thesis is not that it sells inexpensive drones. It is that a shared software layer can coordinate equipment, while a shared production system can lower the cost and time required to manufacture it. If both work, each additional product can benefit from engineering, procurement, integration and manufacturing investments already made for earlier products. That is a plausible source of operating leverage. It is not the same as zero marginal cost.

There is evidence for software that can earn money beyond an Anduril airframe. The company announced an $86 million, three-year mission-autonomy integration contract with Special Operations Command in 2025, and a Lattice selection for NATO’s air-command data platform in July 2026. These establish applications across systems; they do not disclose a clean, recurring software revenue segment with known renewal rates or gross margins. [S13](#source-s13) [S14](#source-s14)

I separate three economic roles. Software sold to customers can generate its own revenue. Software embedded in an Anduril product can improve that product’s price, cost or performance. Internal manufacturing software can improve factory throughput. Counting the same dollar in all three roles is the easiest way to make the valuation look sophisticated and wrong.

For example, faster inspection could reduce work in process and increase output per machine. The benefit belongs in lower working-capital needs, higher margins or less capital expenditure. It does not also justify assigning a freestanding software multiple to an internal tool for which external customer revenue has not been demonstrated. Similarly, an airframe sold with bundled autonomy is one commercial sale unless the customer pays an incremental software charge.

Ramp is a useful conceptual contrast, not a valuation comparable. Its product writing connects transaction visibility to less customer work, then to distribution and monetization. The transferable lesson is to follow the mechanism that earns the money rather than the product label. In Anduril’s case, a sensor feeding a common network may create valuable information, but the investor still needs to know whether the customer pays for that information, for the equipment, or for an integrated service. [S17](#source-s17)

sections.title: The customer wants interoperability, not a new dependency
paragraphs: A common software layer can become strategically important without becoming an unrestricted tollbooth. The Army’s September discussion of the Right to Integrate explicitly favors open interfaces and modular systems, while describing Lattice as an integration tool. That is an opportunity for a capable integrator and a limit on the strongest lock-in story. [S10](#source-s10)

On October 5, Anduril announced an NGC2 award worth up to $1.8 billion over five years, beginning with I Corps. That is stronger evidence than another demonstration: the stated purpose is to move toward operational fielding. But it remains a ceiling, involves an integrated system, and cannot be treated as pure software annual recurring revenue. [S11](#source-s11)

My expectation is a mixed market. Some customers will prefer an integrated Anduril solution because it works sooner with fewer interfaces to manage. Others will separate airframes, autonomy, sensors and command systems to preserve bargaining power. Winning either way is attractive. Earning the same margin either way is not assured.

Interoperability also changes how a moat must be defended. Proprietary interfaces can make a customer expensive to lose; open interfaces force the supplier to remain useful. Anduril can still win through deployment experience, reliability, integration knowledge and qualified production capacity. Those advantages accumulate through execution, but they require continuing engineering and support spending. They are not permission to let the research budget disappear in a spreadsheet.

International expansion presents the same trade-off. Anduril’s announced joint production and sustainment venture with EDGE illustrates a way to reach customers through local capability. Access can improve while ownership of the resulting economics becomes shared. I would value attributable profits, not count every dollar of a partner’s local production as if Anduril owned it outright. [S15](#source-s15)

sections.title: Defense demand is not the bottleneck in the valuation
paragraphs: The bullish demand argument has become more concrete. A May framework described a minimum of 3,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500M systems over three years. The economic question is what those systems cost to deliver, when they are accepted, and how much capital is tied up before payment. The announcement does not supply unit prices or program-level profits. [S16](#source-s16)

The March Army enterprise vehicle is another example. It consolidates more than 120 earlier procurement actions and provides a long-duration purchasing channel. That can shorten sales and contracting work. It does not establish that every permitted order will be placed, and consolidation means some business was already present. Adding the ceiling to existing revenue would count opportunity as cash and risk counting the same business twice. [S5](#source-s5)

I expect spending to move toward systems that are easier to replenish, cheaper to upgrade, and usable across a mixed fleet. That would favor a supplier that can deliver qualified output repeatedly rather than produce an impressive prototype once. It also creates a price-volume tension: greater affordability can enlarge unit demand while reducing revenue per unit. A forecast must choose quantities, prices and margins that can coexist.

The new Steelfin family makes the tension visible. Anduril describes a common interceptor architecture and aims for production in the thousands, but flight testing is planned for 2027. Common components may lower development and production costs; they do not eliminate qualification risk. I count this as a possible source of future growth, not demonstrated high-rate output. [S9](#source-s9)

The central strategic bet is therefore on capital productivity: useful output per dollar invested, not floor space per press release. A plant with spare capacity is valuable when it can accept real orders without another large investment. It is costly when equipment, labor and inventory wait for orders that arrive late. An enormous defense budget does not resolve that distinction.

sections.title: A 22% operating margin is already a demanding assumption
paragraphs: My base case does not value Anduril as an average industrial contractor. It reaches a 22% consolidated operating margin, after continuing development and corporate costs. For context, Lockheed Martin’s Missiles and Fire Control segment reported a 14.1% operating margin for the first half of 2026. Segment profit is not directly comparable with consolidated Anduril EBIT, and the businesses differ. The comparison is a reason to explain the premium assumption, not mechanically borrow a multiple. [S12](#source-s12)

A simple mix test makes the burden explicit. Suppose hardware contributes 15% of revenue after product costs and development, separately monetized software contributes 50%, and unallocated corporate expense consumes 5% of total revenue. A 22% consolidated margin then requires software to represent about 34% of sales. The 28% upside margin requires roughly 51%. These are illustrative contribution assumptions, not disclosed Anduril segments.

Better factories provide another route. Raising hardware contribution to 20% reduces the software share required for a 22% consolidated margin to approximately 23%. That is why manufacturing quality is a valuation driver rather than a secondary operational detail. Anduril does not need to become a pure software company; it needs unusually productive hardware economics, a substantial separate software business, or both.

The arithmetic also explains what would weaken the case. If new revenue is mostly hardware integration with modest contribution, rapid growth can lower the share of high-margin software. Revenue can beat expectations while the valuation disappoints. Conversely, third-party software adoption can create upside that a consolidated revenue growth rate misses. The relevant disclosure is the incremental gross profit earned on a new order, not simply whether the product contains AI.

figures.label: 01 · Margin arithmetic
figures.alt: With hardware contribution of 15%, software contribution of 50%, and corporate expense of 5%, a 22% EBIT margin requires 34% software sales and 28% requires 51%.
figures.caption: A mix test, not reported segment economics. Hardware contribution includes product development; the 5% corporate charge is additional. Software must be separately monetized, not revenue already counted in hardware.

sections.title: The factory belongs in the cash-flow statement
paragraphs: Arsenal-2 makes the financing question harder to ignore. Anduril announced $3.7 billion of private investment alongside a Navy contract of up to $2.9 billion, with payments tied to production outcomes and initial operations expected in 2030. The work is intended to support the existing submarine industrial base, not simply replace the incumbent prime contractors. [S6](#source-s6)

That structure should not be simplified into “the government paid for the factory.” Payment for output compensates the supplier for fulfilling a contract, including the costs of producing it. It is not automatically free capital. Customer advances, reimbursed assets, infrastructure grants and ordinary purchase revenue have different economics. Without their actual terms, netting $2.9 billion against $3.7 billion of investment would invent a financing benefit.

There is also an ownership claim to respect. At the announcement, President Trump said taxpayers would receive a 40% stake in the shipyard. The reviewed record does not establish the completed agreement’s cash-flow rights, priority or valuation. It is a project-level announcement, not evidence that the government owns 40% of Anduril’s parent. [S7](#source-s7)

Accordingly, this model values consolidated operations and labels its equity bridge before minority interests. A finalized outside claim on shipyard cash flows must be deducted at fair value, or the project must be valued on an attributable basis. It would be wrong to deduct 40% of the entire company. It would also be wrong to call the unadjusted bridge common equity value and quietly assume the stake has no cost.

For the base cash forecast I allocate the announced private investment across 2027–2031: $0.60 billion, $0.85 billion, $0.90 billion, $0.85 billion and $0.50 billion. That is my schedule, not management’s. It is additional to ordinary capital expenditure, and it is not reduced by the Navy ceiling. The ordinary capital budget covers other capacity; putting Arsenal-2 inside that budget again would double count it.

The resulting cash trough is approximately $10.5 billion below the valuation date’s starting balance. With an illustrative $3 billion of available cash, the incremental financing need is about $7.5 billion, before financing fees, discretionary acquisitions or a contingency reserve. Net cash for valuation and cash available for operations are separate inputs. Both are assumed here, not observed balances.

This is why the apparent paradox is possible: operating profit turns positive in 2030, but free cash flow remains negative through 2031. Growth requires inventory and receivables as well as factories. The business can be economically successful before it becomes self-financing. A customer advance or project partner could shorten the gap, but the benefit must be earned through an actual agreement, not inserted to make the model balance.

figures.label: 02 · Financing before harvest
figures.alt: Base cumulative free cash flow falls to negative $10.48 billion in 2031 and recovers above zero in 2035; $3 billion of assumed available cash implies a $7.48 billion financing gap at the trough.
figures.caption: Cumulative unlevered cash flow from October 14, 2026, before financing. The shaded $3bn starting-liquidity assumption is not a disclosed cash balance. Annual unlevered FCF first becomes positive in 2032.

sections.title: What the base case actually asks Anduril to accomplish
paragraphs: Revenue rises from the planning anchor to $6.9 billion in 2027, $22.2 billion in 2031 and $50.7 billion in 2036. That is approximately 28% annual growth across a decade. It requires a much larger product portfolio, repeat procurement, qualified supply chains and production capacity far beyond a first aircraft. I do not present the path as a bottom-up estimate of classified contracts. It is an explicit operating outcome to test against price.

EBIT margins progress from a 20% loss in 2027 to 9% in 2031 and 22% in 2036. Ordinary capital expenditure starts at 6% of sales and declines to 3.5%, before the separate Arsenal-2 schedule. Net operating working capital declines from 18% to 14% of sales. That last improvement is favorable: it assumes growth eventually becomes less demanding of cash through better collections, inventory management, supplier terms or customer financing.

The cash equation is NOPAT plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and the increase in net working capital. NOPAT means operating profit after modeled cash tax. I apply a 24% tax rate to positive EBIT and recognize no immediate tax refund on losses. Undisclosed loss carryforwards could postpone future tax, so this convention is conservative. I do not book an additional tax asset on top of the cash forecast.

Development expense remains inside EBIT. So does the economic cost of employee compensation; stock compensation is not added back as free money. Without a cap table, a separate modeled employee-dilution penalty on top of fully expensed compensation would risk charging the same cost twice. New external funding is a different question and should be examined through the capital terms.

The valuation starts on October 14, not January 1. Only 78/365 of the annualized 2026 cash-flow proxy is included, approximately negative $0.53 billion. That is a pro-rata stub assumption, not a claim that defense collections occur evenly through the year. Full calendar-year cash flows begin in 2027. Spending that occurred before the valuation date is not charged a second time.

table.note: Author assumptions and calculations. Cash tax, depreciation and every annual row are in the downloadable model; these selected years are not a full cash-flow reconciliation.

sections.title: The result is about $28 billion of operating value
paragraphs: I discount the cash flows at 12%. That is an underwriting assumption for execution and financing risk, not a statistically estimated private-company cost of capital. After 2036, growth fades over five years to 3%. Reinvestment gradually converges to the amount needed to sustain a 15% return on new invested capital in the base case. This avoids pretending that a business can grow forever without paying for additional capital.

Terminal free cash flow equals next-year NOPAT multiplied by one minus terminal growth divided by return on invested capital. At 3% growth and 15% returns, 20% of NOPAT must be reinvested. The remaining 80% can support capital providers. A higher perpetual growth rate is therefore not a free increase in value; it consumes more reinvestment as well.

The base case produces $27.7 billion of consolidated enterprise value. About 66% comes from the terminal period after 2041. That dependence is a warning about precision: a decimal place in the output does not turn uncertain economics fifteen years away into a measured asset.

With $3 billion of assumed net cash, the gross equity bridge is $30.7 billion. At the same operating assumptions, reducing the discount rate to 10% raises that bridge to $46.7 billion; raising it to 14% lowers it to $21.1 billion. These are parameter sensitivities, not confidence intervals. Net cash then changes value dollar for dollar, as does any deduction for outside or senior claims.

The upside case reaches $74.9 billion of sales in 2036, 28% operating margins and 20% mature returns on new capital. It yields approximately $67.4 billion of enterprise value, or $70.4 billion on the same unadjusted gross equity bridge. The $61 billion financing price sits much closer to that outcome than to the base case.

The downside case still grows sales to $17.1 billion in 2036 and achieves a 15% operating margin. Yet the present value of operations is approximately zero after the modeled investment and losses. Its $2.9 billion gross equity bridge should not be read as a recoverable cash floor: management could cancel projects, financing could fail, and security priorities would determine recoveries. A near-zero continuation value is a reason to change the capital plan, not a claim that a limited-liability share can have a negative price.

sections.title: What would make $61 billion reasonable?
paragraphs: Holding base-case margins, returns on capital and discounting constant, the reverse DCF requires approximately $99.5 billion of annual sales in 2036 to support the $61 billion gross equity reference. That is almost twice the base-case revenue outcome and about 37% annual growth from the planning anchor. The $100 billion reference requires approximately $162.9 billion of 2036 sales, or 44% annual growth.

Those are lower-bound price tests with respect to undisclosed outside claims: they include the same $3 billion net-cash assumption and no minority-interest deduction. The reverse model scales each annual growth factor rather than simply inflating the final year. Earlier revenue, losses and investment move with the larger business. The code exposes the transformation.

This is not a prediction that either revenue figure is impossible. It identifies what must change in the argument. To pay $61 billion without underwriting that much sales, an investor needs higher margins, better capital productivity, a lower required return, more favorable financing, or additional cash-flow sources not already included. The upside scenario demonstrates a combination that works; “defense spending is going up” does not supply the missing assumptions.

A second test concerns investor returns rather than intrinsic value. At a hypothetical 15% annual return target, an investor entering at $61 billion needs an equity value of about $308 billion ten years later if the original stake suffers 20% cumulative dilution and receives no interim distributions. At a $100 billion entry, the hurdle is approximately $506 billion. The calculation is entry value × 1.15¹⁰ ÷ 0.80. These are illustrative exit-equity hurdles, not terminal enterprise values or a second adjustment to the DCF.

The funding requirement is already charged through negative free cash flow in the DCF. Subtracting all future financing proceeds or imposing a blanket dilution haircut on top would be wrong. Financing terms matter because capital may be raised above or below fair value, may carry preferences, and may restrict what existing shareholders receive. Fresh capital creates cash at the same time that it creates a new claim.

figures.label: 05 · The price expressed as revenue
figures.alt: At base operating economics, the $61 billion gross equity reference requires $99.5 billion of 2036 sales and the $100 billion reference requires $162.9 billion, versus $50.7 billion in the base scenario.
figures.caption: Reverse DCF at 12% discount rate, 22% mature EBIT margin, 15% mature return on new capital, and 3% terminal growth. Same $3bn net-cash assumption; no minority-interest deduction. This is a conditional hurdle, not a revenue forecast.

sections.title: The evidence that would change my price
paragraphs: The most valuable new disclosure would be a cash-flow statement tied to funded orders. I would look for accepted shipments, gross profit after warranty and rework, and cash conversion after customer advances. An order book that grows faster than inventory is different from a factory filling with unfinished systems while revenue recognition waits for acceptance.

Next is separately monetized software. Renewals, third-party deployments and software gross profit would support a higher margin path. Merely renaming a bundled hardware contract as a platform deal would not. Factory evidence should be equally specific: accepted units per machine-hour, first-pass yield, time in process, and incremental capital required for another dollar of qualified output.

Arsenal-2 requires its own financing and ownership reconciliation. Final project terms could reveal customer financing that reduces Anduril’s burden, or cash-flow rights that reduce the parent’s upside. Either can change value materially. A subsidy with conditions is not the same asset as unrestricted cash; a stake in a project is not a stake in the parent.

I would also watch whether Anduril can remain selective. A rapidly expanding contractor can win too much work at the wrong price, stretch qualified suppliers, and turn growth into a financing problem. Capital allocation means refusing a prestigious project when its incremental return is poor, even when the addressable market is large.

My forecast is that Anduril becomes more industrial as it becomes more important. More products, more integrations and more manufacturing capability can reinforce the software advantage, but they also expose the company to the same disciplines that govern every scaled producer: yield, utilization, collections and return on capital. The interesting future is not software replacing the factory. It is software making the factory economically better.

At approximately $61 billion, I would require evidence closer to the upside case before treating the financing price as an attractive underwriting entry. Around the base case’s $28 billion enterprise value, the argument is different: investors are paying for a large, unusually profitable defense business while retaining some benefit if the platform economics become stronger. Anduril may earn the higher price. The work is to distinguish earning it from announcing it.
